posts.quote: A NICKEL AT THE PENNY CANDY COUNTER BOUGHT TEN DECISIONS AND ONE PAPER BAG.
posts.caption: Every kid knew the walk to the corner store with a nickel clutched in a sweaty fist. The candy sat in glass jars along the counter, and the shopkeeper waited with a paper bag and endless patience. You pointed at a licorice whip, changed your mind, pointed at a gumball, changed it again. Two cents here, three cents there, and the whole thing had to be figured out before the nickel ran dry. By the time you walked out, the bag was light and the decision felt like the biggest one of your week.
posts.first: My brother and I used to pool our nickels so we could buy a little of everything and split it on the front steps. He always traded away his black licorice before we got home. I still think about how serious the two of us were at that counter.

posts.quote: The best part of a snow day was the kitchen radio reading the school closings, one name at a time.
posts.first: We sat around the table in our pajamas with the toast going cold, listening for our town. When they finally said it, my mother just shook her head and smiled. I can still hear that announcer's voice.

posts.quote: THE DRUGSTORE COUNTER HAD SPINNING STOOLS, A CHROME MALT MACHINE, AND A CHERRY PHOSPHATE FOR A DIME.
posts.caption: The soda fountain sat at the back of the drugstore, right past the greeting cards and the cough syrup. The stools were red vinyl and they spun, which was the whole reason for sitting on one. A soda jerk in a paper hat worked a row of chrome spigots like a man playing the organ. Cherry phosphates came in tall glasses with a long spoon and a paper straw. After Saturday errands, the drugstore counter was where the whole town slowed down for ten minutes.
posts.first: My mother let me have one cherry phosphate every Saturday if I stayed quiet through the whole grocery trip. I never once stayed quiet, and I got it anyway. She would sip her coffee and pretend not to notice me spinning.

posts.quote: THE KIDS' TABLE WAS A CARD TABLE IN THE HALLWAY, AND WE HAD THE BETTER TIME.
posts.caption: Thanksgiving meant two tables, and you knew which one you belonged to the minute you walked in. The grown-ups got the good china and the dining room. The cousins got a wobbly card table in the hallway, folding chairs, and paper napkins. Somebody always got the drumstick by mistake and nobody argued. We laughed so loud that Grandma finally came to the doorway and shushed us, and then she stayed a minute to listen.
posts.first: I was the youngest cousin, so I sat on the phone book. Nobody ever told me it was a promotion when I finally got moved to the big table. I think I missed the hallway for a long time after that.

posts.quote: PENMANSHIP / LOOPS, SLANTS, AND A GOLD STAR FOR A STEADY HAND
posts.caption: Penmanship class started with a sheet of lined paper and a row of looping circles. The teacher walked the aisles checking the slant of every letter against the alphabet strip above the chalkboard. Your wrist ached, your tongue stuck out in concentration, and the capital Q seemed designed to ruin your afternoon. A gold star on the corner of the page felt like a medal. Somewhere in a shoebox there is still a thank-you note written in that careful hand.
posts.first: My mother's handwriting looked like it came off a typewriter. She said the nuns made her redo whole pages until every loop closed. I still keep a recipe card in her writing, and it makes me sit up straighter.

posts.quote: GRANDPA'S POCKET WATCH GOT WOUND EVERY NIGHT, AND IT NEVER ONCE RAN LATE.
posts.caption: Grandpa wound his pocket watch every night after supper, three slow turns of the little brass crown. Then he set it on the nightstand next to his reading glasses and a folded handkerchief. The watch had a scratch on the face from a day in the machine shop that he never would let anybody repair. When you leaned close, you could hear it ticking steady as a heartbeat. Nobody in that house was ever late, and now you know why.
posts.first: He let me hold it once, and I was afraid to breathe. It was heavier than it looked, and still warm from his vest pocket. I kept my hand perfectly still until he took it back.

posts.quote: A kitchen light left on at night meant somebody was still on the way home.
posts.first: My mother never went to bed until she heard the car in the driveway. She would turn the light off after, and that was how I knew everyone was in. It was the quietest kind of love I ever saw.

posts.quote: MOM CUT OUR HAIR AT THE KITCHEN TABLE WITH A MIXING BOWL AND A STRAIGHT FACE.
posts.caption: Haircuts at our house happened on a kitchen chair with a bath towel pinned around your neck. Mom set the mixing bowl on your head like a crown and went around the edge with the good scissors. You were told to hold still, and you did, because she was holding the scissors. When she finished, she brushed off your neck and declared you handsome. The bangs were always a little crooked, and you wore them proudly all week.
posts.first: My brother and I got the bowl treatment until I was ten. I came home from school one day and Dad had a straight line of tape on the floor to keep our chairs lined up. That was the whole system, and it worked.

posts.quote: MILK MONEY / A NICKEL IN AN ENVELOPE AND A COLD BOTTLE AT MORNING RECESS
posts.caption: Monday morning meant a nickel tucked into an envelope with your name printed on the front. You handed it to the teacher and she checked you off on a clipboard. At recess the milk crate came out, and every kid got a small cold bottle with a cardboard cap. The cream sat at the top and the first sip made a white mustache. It tasted better than anything on earth, mostly because it was cold and you got to drink it in the sunshine.
posts.first: My teacher always poured the cream line into a cup for the kid who looked hungriest. She never said anything, and none of us ever mentioned it. I remember that more than the milk itself.

posts.quote: DAD TAUGHT ME TO TIE MY SHOES ONE EVENING, AND HE NEVER ONCE RAISED HIS VOICE.
posts.caption: It was a summer evening on the front steps, and Dad had just come in from work. He sat next to me with his tie loosened and showed me the bunny ears one more time. My loops kept falling apart and I wanted to quit three times. Each time he just undid the knot and said we would try it once more. When the bow finally held, he didn't say a word, he just gave my shoe a little pat.
posts.first: I tied my shoes in front of the whole class the next morning to show off. The teacher gave me a nod and I thought I was the best boy in the school. I owe that to a quiet evening and a very patient father.
